title: Extraterrestrial signals taken for noise could be meaningful messages

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Extraterrestrial signals taken for noise could be meaningful messages

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Some extraterrestrial radio and other signals that are detected and assumed to be random noise could be meaningful messages encoded in a way recognizable only by higher forms of perception and analysis than those applied so far.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: it seems far from inconceivable that some of the extraterrestrial radio and other signals that we pick up and assume to be random noise could in fact be meaningful messages

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 10, “Processes of Perception and Analysis”; section “Higher Forms of Perception and Analysis” (from p. 632), p. 635. Scope: astronomical radio and other signals searched for extraterrestrial intelligence

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch10-25: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.42

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Large public radio datasets make many concrete searches possible now. The existential, open-ended wording and indistinguishability of sufficiently unfamiliar encoding from noise prevent a decisive resolution of the full claim.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Reanalyze public SETI recordings with prespecified searches for decodable, information-bearing structure beyond standard narrowband and transient detectors. A reproducible signal with non-natural encoding and independent recurrence would support the claim; null searches constrain only the searched encoding classes.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Available observations cover a tiny fraction of sources, times, frequencies, and signal types.

Meaningfulness is not identifiable from arbitrary ciphertext-like noise without a key.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.75
analysis feasibility: 0.45
discriminating power: 0.2
data adequacy: 0.35
operationalizability: 0.3

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Large public radio archives now exist, so a search for particular simple encodings is an ordinary reanalysis. That search can confirm the claim if it recovers a message, but it cannot refute the possibility claim, which is why discriminating power stays low. Coverage is also only the recorded targets and bands, not every extraterrestrial signal that has been set aside as noise.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Search public radio spectra and time series, already treated as noise, for a pre-specified family of simple encodings such as a cellular-automaton row or a short program. Decoding even one signal as such a message would support the claim; failing to decode it would not refute it, because the encoding is otherwise unspecified.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Arbitrary higher encodings are not a finite search; only a pre-registered family can be tested.

The claim is existential and the encoding is not specified, so every undecoded record is compatible both with noise and with an unrecognized message.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

analysis feasibility: 0.4
discriminating power: 0.2
data adequacy: 0.45
operationalizability: 0.35
